sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Patrick is the name of the Irish saint and missionary bishop who came to Ireland in the fifth century. Koch records him as a third-generation Christian from Roman Britain, not yet a firm believer. His family held slaves and owned a house and a farm near the town of Bannaventa. Latin was not his first language, and his broken schooling left him weak in it. When he was about sixteen, Irish slave raiders took him with his father's servants and thousands more into Ireland. Six years of slavery followed. He tended livestock alone, and in that hardship he came to faith. A voice told him to escape, and he walked a great distance to reach a ship. He boarded only after refusing a rough rite. The crew landed in a desolate place and lost the way. They nearly starved until Patrick found food. He reached his family safely in Britain. Scholars still dispute whether he spent time in Gaul during the quiet years after. Later, in a vivid dream, a man named Victoricius appeared bearing many letters. He is sometimes linked with the bishop of Rouen. In that vision Patrick read the voice of the Irish people calling him home. He sailed back in the role of missionary bishop, travelling the land and bringing many people to the faith. Two works by him survive, the Confessio and the Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus. Two dark threads run through his story. First, he faced financial suspicion. He paid the sons of Irish rulers to ride with him as a safe escort, yet he refused all offerings. Second, his writing held an apocalyptic side. In the letter he scolded raiders who had slain recent converts, abducted the women, and sold them to the Picts. He also cut off those half-hearted Christians. Muirchu's Vita, from about 690, gives him four names. It tells of service to a druid. It records time in Gaul. It also gives a night of Easter near Tara and a meeting with King Loegaire. It also names Armagh as his church. The annals give two dates for his death, near 462 and near 493. Binchy's scholarly essay was a turning point. It showed that much later detail served the politics of its own age. So the saint of legend far outreached the modest man of the letters.

okr.objective: Patrick is the Irish saint and missionary bishop of the fifth century whose own works and later legend both shaped his fame.
